1. Core Clinical Tension: A 41-year-old male active smoker with a paternal history of lung cancer presents with a 3-week history of exertional dyspnea, occasional wheezing, 6 months of intermittent diarrhea, a chronic 5-year nonproductive cough, and a large left-sided spontaneous pneumothorax with persistent air leak requiring multiple chest tubes. The central diagnostic challenge is differentiating between primary spontaneous pneumothorax, pulmonary tuberculosis, bronchogenic malignancy, bacterial empyema, and systemic eosinophilic pulmonary syndromes in the context of marked, rising peripheral eosinophilia (AEC up to 1,210.2 cells/µL) and a history of Missouri river recreation with wild game and freshwater crustacean exposure.

2. Admission Breakpoint: The teaching case presentation strictly halts at the initial hospitalization and preoperative surgical workup—incorporating the clinical history, exposure history along the Missouri River, triage vitals, physical examination, initial radiographs and CT imaging demonstrating pneumothorax with pleural thickening and slow lung re-expansion, serial CBC differentials confirming marked eosinophilia, and normal preoperative flexible bronchoscopy—prior to video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) tissue biopsy, histopathological identification of trematode eggs, definitive diagnosis of Paragonimus kellicotti infection, or initiation of praziquantel therapy.

3. Differential Distinctions: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax was the initial working surgical hypothesis but cannot account for marked peripheral eosinophilia, chronic 5-year cough, preceding hemoptysis, or dense intrapleural fibrin and granulomatous inflammation. Pulmonary tuberculosis commonly causes secondary pneumothorax and chronic hemoptysis but classically elicits lymphocytic rather than marked eosinophilic responses. Bronchogenic malignancy is a high concern given 30 pack-years of tobacco use and paternal lung cancer, but is excluded by normal bronchoscopy and negative histopathology. Bacterial empyema is ruled out by sterile pleural fluid cultures and lack of high fever. The diagnostic pivot hinges on connecting the marked peripheral eosinophilia (11.3%, AEC 1,210.2 cells/µL) with the patient's lifelong Missouri residence and Missouri River hunting/rafting exposure involving wild game and potential crayfish consumption, pointing directly to endemic pulmonary paragonimiasis (Foodborne Trematodes).
case_prompt:
A 41-year-old male with no prior medical history presented to an urgent care clinic at an outside hospital with dyspnea (worse on exertion) and occasional wheezing for three weeks, accompanied by intermittent diarrhea for the preceding six months. He also reported a chronic nonproductive cough for the previous five years and noted a recent streptococcal throat infection in his daughter. He was an active cigarette smoker with a 30 pack-year history, with occasional marijuana and beer intake. His family history was significant for lung cancer in his father.

Social and exposure history revealed that he had lived in Missouri for most of his life and worked at his own moving company. He recalled participating in a hunting and river-rafting trip five years earlier along the Missouri River, during which he consumed alcohol and wild boar meat cooked overnight; on this trip, his companions consumed cooked crayfish, although he denied intentional crayfish intake. Approximately three months after that river excursion, he experienced a productive cough with minimal clear white phlegm and hemoptysis that persisted for about 12 months, which subsequently resolved into his persistent chronic cough.

On physical examination, the patient was mildly tachycardic with a heart rate of 109 beats per minute, but other vital signs were stable. Pulmonary examination demonstrated an absence of lung sounds over the left hemithorax. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

Chest radiography (CXR, two views) revealed a large left-sided pneumothorax without tension physiology. He was immediately transferred to the emergency department, where a 20-French chest tube was inserted into the left fourth intercostal space, and he was admitted to the inpatient surgical service. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed a normal complete metabolic panel. Complete blood cell count with differential (CBCD) demonstrated an elevated eosinophil percentage of 5.9% with an absolute eosinophil count (AEC) of 610.7 cells/µL.

Repeat radiographs showed slow lung re-expansion, and subsequent chest computed tomography (CT) displayed persistent pneumothorax with pleural thickening and inflammation. Despite repositioning and placement of smaller-caliber chest tubes connected to a Heimlich valve, repeat radiographs following tube clamping demonstrated persistent left apical pneumothorax and an ongoing air leak. A repeat CBCD on hospital day three revealed worsening peripheral eosinophilia of 11.3% with an AEC of 1,210.2 cells/µL.

Because of the persistent air leak spanning three weeks, he was evaluated by cardiothoracic surgery with a primary working impression of primary spontaneous pneumothorax and was scheduled for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) pleurodesis and wedge resection. Preoperative flexible bronchoscopy was performed and was entirely normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially considered the primary clinical diagnosis by the cardiothoracic surgical team given the patient's smoking history and large unilateral pneumothorax with persistent air leak requiring chest tube drainage and scheduled VATS pleurodesis. However, primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs from the rupture of apical subpleural blebs in otherwise healthy lung parenchyma and fails to explain marked peripheral eosinophilia (11.3%, AEC 1,210.2 cells/µL), prolonged cough with antecedent hemoptysis, or intraoperative extensive chronic granulomatous inflammation with dense intrapleural fibrin.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The primary impression was of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax with persistent air leak for the last three weeks. He was scheduled for a Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) pleurodesis via pleurectomy and likely wedge resection of the lung bulla the next day.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as an important infectious cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, chronic cough, preceding hemoptysis, and chronic granulomatous inflammation on pleural biopsy. However, uncomplicated pulmonary tuberculosis characteristically produces a lymphocytic rather than prominent eosinophilic response, whereas this patient exhibited marked peripheral eosinophilia (AEC > 1,200 cells/µL), and tissue histopathology demonstrated parasitic trematode ova rather than caseating granulomas or acid-fast bacilli.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: LLL and LUL wedge resection and left parietal pleura histopathology revealed multiple parasite eggs (consistent with Paragonimus kellicotti), severe chronic granulomatous inflammation with fibrosis, negative for malignancy and changes consistent with pneumothorax

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered a serious possibility given the patient's 30 pack-year smoking history, family history of lung cancer in his father, chronic 5-year cough, prior hemoptysis, and secondary pneumothorax. However, preoperative flexible bronchoscopy was completely normal, and pathological examination of surgical wedge resections from both the left upper and lower lobes as well as the parietal pleura was definitively negative for malignancy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: His family history was significant for lung cancer in his father... He underwent preoperative flexible bronchoscopy, which was normal... negative for malignancy and changes consistent with pneumothorax

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to pleural thickening, dense intrapleural fibrin requiring surgical debridement, persistent air leak, and recent streptococcal infection in a family contact. However, the patient lacked high fevers or leukocytic toxic shift, chest tube drainage was clear yellow (30–100 mL/day) without frank purulence, empirical antibacterial therapy (oral cephalexin and amoxicillin-clavulanate) did not resolve the condition, bacterial cultures of pleural fluid and fibrin were sterile, and marked peripheral eosinophilia is uncharacteristic of pyogenic bacterial infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Left anterior pleural fluid and fibrin samples were sent for culture... with the chest tube draining clear yellow drainage of 30 mL/day.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA) / Hypereosinophilic Syndrome
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered in light of the patient's striking peripheral eosinophilia (11.3%, AEC 1,210.2 cells/µL), 3 weeks of wheezing and exertional dyspnea, 6 months of intermittent diarrhea, and pulmonary parenchymal involvement. However, the patient had no antecedent history of adult-onset asthma, atopy, allergic rhinitis, cutaneous vasculitic lesions, or peripheral neuropathy, his metabolic panel was normal, and lung biopsy revealed parasitic eggs rather than necrotizing vasculitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A CBCD on day three showed elevated eosinophils of 11.3 % with an AEC of 1210.2 cells/microL... whereas the complete metabolic panel was normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Foodborne Trematodes (Pulmonary Paragonimiasis / Paragonimus kellicotti)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive diagnostic pivot combines persistent secondary spontaneous pneumothorax and chronic pleuropulmonary symptoms with marked peripheral eosinophilia (11.3%, AEC 1,210.2 cells/µL) and an endemic epidemiological exposure: long-term Missouri residency and a river-rafting/hunting excursion along the Missouri River with ingestion of wild game and potential crustacean (crayfish) contamination, the obligate secondary intermediate host of Paragonimus kellicotti. Definitive confirmation was established when lung wedge resection histopathology identified characteristic trematode eggs within chronic granulomatous tissue, leading to complete clinical resolution following oral praziquantel therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He recalled going on a hunting and river rafting trip five years ago along the Missouri river... On this trip, his wife and friends ate cooked crayfish... LLL and LUL wedge resection and left parietal pleura histopathology revealed multiple parasite eggs (consistent with Paragonimus kellicotti)... The patient was started on praziquantel 600 mg orally three times a day for three days
